newsitem.title: USA: Decision on Zaire force expected this week.
newsitem.headline: Decision on Zaire force expected this week.

text.p: Military officials from Canada, the United States and about a dozen other nations will meet in Germany on Thursday to assess the rapidly changing need for a humanitarian relief force in Zaire, the Pentagon said on Monday.

Representatives of nations that have offered to send troops to support a U.N.-authorised relief effort in Zaire and possibly Rwanda will meet at U.S. European military headquarters in Stuttgart, Army Lt. Col. Nancy Burt, a Pentagon spokeswoman, said.

"I expect something to come out on Thursday," she said, adding that the meeting would be attended by Canadian Army Lt. Gen. Marice Baril, who has been designated to head a military task force to help refugees in Zaire.

Although tens of thousands of refugees in Zaire have returned to Rwanda in recent days, U.S. officials stressed privately that there was still need for humanitarian relief for those remaining in Zaire. The question, they said, was how much military support would be needed to assure distribution of food and other aid either in Zaire or Rwanda.
The meeting in Stuttgart, which will also include representatives from Britain and France, will study a detailed report from military assessment teams already in Zaire and Rwanda.

President Bill Clinton last week tentatively offered 1,000 U.S. troops to move into Goma, Zaire, and another 2,000 or 3,000 support troops to be based in nearby countries. But Defence Secretary William Perry said over the weekend that the sudden flow of refugees home to Rwanda had changed the picture and that a decision would be made this week.
"I think every country (that has offered troops) has a different idea of what they want to do," said one Pentagon official, who asked not to be identified.

Pentagon officials said U.S. Air Force cargo planes and crews had already been moved to Moron Air Base in Spain to take part in a potential "air bridge" to central Africa and that other planes could be moved quickly to countries near Zaire after diplomatic arrangements are made.

Robert Oakley, the former U.S. ambassador to Zaire, said on Sunday that a military mission was needed in any event to help refugees in the southern part of Zaire. He said there were "300,000-400,000 refugees in south Zaire who can't get back because of intimidation and it seems the sort of operation envisaged for the north and south needs to be carried out in the south."
